newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US rates steady in Q4, dip in '97 - experts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US rates steady in Q4, dip in '97 - experts.

text.p: U.S. long-term interest rates will plateau just below current levels through yearend as U.S. credit markets anticipate slower economic growth, according to the results of a Reuters poll of U.S. economists.

On average, 31 experts surveyed on Wednesday and Thursday forecast the 30-year Treasury bond yield would dip to 7.07 percent in October and hold nearby before dropping to 6.95 in the first quarter of 1997.
Many economists calling for declining bond yields said the Federal Reserve would raise short-term rates in either September or November to discourage inflation.
That move would pressure the interest rate-sensitive sectors of the economy and eventually slow gross domestic product growth, said Donald Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc.

"You'll see the rate of growth slow down to around 2.0 percent over the first half of next year," Maude said. "That will start taking pressure off of rates when it is perceived as a genuine deceleration."
The Commerce Department's most recent estimate pegged second-quarter gross domestic product growth at a speedy 4.8 percent, up from 2.0 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
Despite the GDP revision from an advance estimate of 4.2 percent, economists said they could already see signs pointing to a slowdown.

"We're looking for auto sales to be weaker, housing starts to be weaker and government purchases to be weaker, and (that) should make for modest growth of about 1.5 percent in the current quarter," said Kurt Karl, chief economist for U.S. forecasting at WEFA Group.
Karl projected the long-bond's yield would dip below 7.0 percent by October 1 and then sink gradually to 5.9 percent over the coming year.
That scenario depends on moderate inflation going forward, Karl said.
"We see no change in inflation," he said. "We have the CPI (Consumer Price Index) hovering close to, but not quite at, 3.0 percent."
Respondents projecting an initial rise in long-term rates before a decline in 1997 said yields would fall after tighter monetary policy restrains growth.
Bill Sharp, an economist at Smith Barney Inc, said GDP probably will slow some time in the second half of next year. But rates should come in before then, he said.
Slower growth "would be anticipated by the (bond) market sometime around the second quarter," he said.
Sharp forecast the bond yield would rise to 7.3 percent by December 1 and stay there at least into March 1997 before moving back toward 7.0 percent.
The experts forecast the two-year note yield would fall in a similar fashion but not as far, leading to a flatter Treasury yield curve.

On average, the analysts projected the two-year rate would level near 6.3 percent in the next month and hold steady into the second quarter of 1997. It should slip moderately thereafter, to about 6.2 percent, they said.
Full results of the survey follow.
